question: How do you preprocess and index private or current documents so an LLM application can retrieve the relevant parts as context?
contributions: Walks the ingestion pipeline: load documents, split into chunks, embed, store in a vector store
Shows the LangChain indexing API (RecordManager) for syncing changing documents
Introduces three indexing optimisations: MultiVectorRetriever, RAPTOR and ColBERT

limits: No experiments or retrieval-quality measurements: every setting is a tutorial example, not a tuned or evaluated value.
The chapter says naive splitting 'leads to inconsistent retrieval results and a relatively high occurrence of hallucinations' without evidence.
RAPTOR and ColBERT get a paragraph each and the RAPTOR section has no code.
Vector store disadvantages listed (new, learning curve, extra system) are asserted, not measured; pgvector is presented as an option, not a recommendation.
Code uses 2024-2025 LangChain import paths and a gpt-3.5-turbo model, and contains typos (e.g. db.delete(ids=[1]), JS 'embeddings.embedDocuments' before definition).
practices: Embed multiple documents in one embed_documents call rather than one at a time, because it is more efficient (Generating Text Embeddings).
Never compare or combine embeddings from different models (TIP, LLM-Based Embeddings).
Store both the original text and its embedding because embeddings are lossy (Embeddings: Converting Text to Numbers).
Choose a vector store by multitenancy, metadata filtering, performance, cost and scalability (Storing Embeddings in a Vector Store).
Consider pgvector to avoid running a separate database (Storing Embeddings in a Vector Store).
Use the indexing API with a RecordManager and a cleanup mode to avoid re-embedding and duplicates when documents change (Tracking Changes to Your Documents).
Use less chunk overlap for code, which is more structured than prose (Splitting Your Text into Chunks).
Pass a metadata list to create_documents so each chunk keeps its source (Splitting Your Text into Chunks).
For documents with tables, embed summaries and keep the raw table in a docstore linked by id (MultiVectorRetriever).

terms.definition: the process of converting your documents into numbers that computers can understand and analyze, and storing them in a special type of database for efficient retrieval
representing text as a (long) sequence of numbers; a lossy representation
word-count vectors where most entries are 0, with no awareness of meaning
lists of floating-point numbers, usually 100 to 2,000 dimensions, where usually all dimensions are non-zero
dot product of vectors divided by the product of their magnitudes, giving a number between -1 and 1
a database designed to store vectors and perform complex calculations like cosine similarity efficiently and quickly
terms.where: Storing Embeddings in a Vector Store

terms.definition: hard limit on input and output tokens a model can handle, usually applying to their combination
terms.where: TIP, Converting Your Documents into Text

terms.definition: the date beyond which the LLM has no knowledge of real-world events, usually when the training set was finalized
class that tracks document writes into the vector store: document hash (content and metadata), write time and source ID
recursive abstractive processing for tree-organized retrieval: summarise, embed and cluster documents, then summarise each cluster recursively, indexing summaries and originals together
per-token contextual embeddings; document score is the sum over query tokens of the maximum similarity to any document token
